narrative:
The model estimates a 47% chance that you will leave your job. Because this probability is high enough to flag risk, the company has decided to deny your promotion.

The decision was driven mainly by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your total years of experience across all jobs had the strongest influence, but it pulled the prediction toward staying rather than leaving. Most employees the model expects to stay also have 1–5 years of experience, so in this respect you look similar to people who remain with their employers.

What pushed the prediction upward toward leaving were the next two factors. You have received other job offers while working here, and the model sees this as a clear signal that you have attractive outside options. In contrast, only 23% of employees predicted to stay had received such offers. The third factor is your sector. Working in “other” rather than in medical or education fields also nudged the prediction toward leaving, as people in those two sectors are more likely to remain.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and your industry outweighed the stabilizing effect of your experience, leading the model to conclude you are at elevated risk of departure. 

The organization should discuss with you whether those external offers can be matched or whether changes in your role would increase your commitment. You, in turn, may want to reflect on what would make staying the clearly better choice.
